title: A Truth Universally Acknowledged
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen (1813).
body: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

"My dear Mr. Bennet," said his lady to him one day, "have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?" Mr. Bennet replied that he had not. "But it is," returned she; "for Mrs. Long has just been here, and she told me all about it." Mr. Bennet made no answer. "Do not you want to know who has taken it?" cried his wife, impatiently. "You want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it."

"Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says that Netherfield is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much delighted with it that he agreed with Mr. Morris immediately; that he is to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be in the house by the end of next week." "What is his name?" "Bingley." "Is he married or single?" "Oh, single, my dear, to be sure! A single man of large fortune; four or five thousand a year. What a fine thing for our girls!"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what "truth" does the opening line claim is universally acknowledged?
options: That a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife
That a woman with a good fortune must remain unmarried
That all wealthy families eventually move to the countryside
That marriage is never discussed among wealthy families

questions.prompt: Per the passage, who told Mrs. Bennet about Netherfield Park being let?
options: Mrs. Long
Mr. Bennet
Mr. Morris
Bingley himself

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what news does Mrs. Bennet bring to her husband?
options: That Netherfield Park is let at last
That their daughter has become engaged
That Mr. Morris has died
That a ball is being planned nearby

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what is the name of the man who has taken Netherfield?
options: Bingley
Bennet
Morris
Long

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the new tenant travel to see Netherfield?
options: He came down on Monday in a chaise and four
He arrived on foot after a long journey
He sailed up the nearby river
He was carried in on horseback alone

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what is the new tenant's fortune, according to Mrs. Bennet?
options: Four or five thousand a year
Ten thousand a year
A few hundred a year
An unknown, unstated amount

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the narrator say the wealthy single man is considered "the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters," regardless of his own feelings?
options: The narrator is being ironic, mocking how local families view a wealthy bachelor purely as a marriage prospect for their daughters
The narrator is stating a literal legal rule of the time
The narrator believes the man has no say in his own life at all
The narrator is warning readers that the man is dangerous

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does Mr. Bennet reply, "You want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it," instead of directly asking who has taken Netherfield?
options: He is teasingly indifferent, letting his wife reveal news she is clearly eager to share
He genuinely has no interest in hearing any news at all
He already knows the full story and is testing her honesty
He is angry with his wife and refuses to speak further

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: A wealthy new bachelor's arrival in the neighborhood immediately excites Mrs. Bennet's hopes for her daughters' marriage prospects
Mr. Bennet is planning to sell his own estate to Bingley
Mrs. Bennet is upset that a stranger has moved into the area
The Bennet family is preparing to leave their home permanently

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that a man is "in want of" a wife?
options: In need of, or lacking, a wife
Actively avoiding a wife
Already married to a wife
Forbidden from having a wife

questions.prompt: According to the passage, had Mr. Bennet already heard about Netherfield being let?
options: No, he replied that he had not
Yes, he had heard it from Mr. Morris
Yes, he had heard it from Bingley directly
The passage does not say

questions.prompt: Per the passage, from where does the new tenant come?
options: The north of England
The south of France
Scotland
London

questions.prompt: According to the passage, by when is the new tenant to take possession of Netherfield?
options: Before Michaelmas
Before Christmas
Before the new year
Before the following summer

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what does Mrs. Bennet exclaim about the meaning of Bingley's fortune for her daughters?
options: "What a fine thing for our girls!"
"What a terrible loss for our girls!"
"Our girls will never meet him!"
"Our girls are too young to marry!"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might Mrs. Bennet be so eager to share every detail about Bingley immediately?
options: She is excited by the prospect of a wealthy, single new neighbor as a marriage opportunity for her daughters
She wants to warn her husband that Bingley is dangerous
She is worried that Bingley will compete with Mr. Bennet's business
She has already decided to move her family away from the area

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes the exchange between Mr. and Mrs. Bennet in the passage?
options: Mrs. Bennet excitedly delivers news of a wealthy new neighbor while Mr. Bennet responds with dry, teasing indifference
Mr. and Mrs. Bennet argue bitterly about their daughters' futures
Mr. Bennet is the one who first brings up the news about Netherfield
Mrs. Bennet refuses to tell her husband any details at all

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does "fortune" refer to when describing the new tenant?
options: His wealth or financial means
His personal reputation among neighbors
His physical appearance
His family's history in the region
